Consult Summary:
- 27-year-old male with 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhea (~hourly when awake), intermittent lower central abdominal cramping, nausea with one episode of vomiting (worse after milk), and subjective fever; likely acute gastroenteritis. Supportive care advised.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Watery diarrhea for ~3 days, occurring nearly every hour when awake.
- Associated symptoms: Intermittent crampy lower central abdominal pain (comes and goes; patient-rated approx. 6/10), nausea, one episode of vomiting after milk, feeling “hot”/febrile, decreased urine frequency. No blood in stool reported.
- Pertinent negatives: No hematochezia reported. Able to take some solids (lunch) but stools remain loose. No clear food trigger identified. Brother has had similar illness for ~5 days and is improving (does not live with patient).
- Past medical history: Denies significant medical history.
- Medications: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) used recently for symptoms; dose/route/frequency not documented. No regular medications.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Family history: Father with colon cancer (patient believes “stage 3,” exact details unknown).
- Social history: Lives with mother and sister. Works in a government office in Central London. Smokes socially (occasional, e.g., Fridays). Alcohol: occasional beers on weekdays; heavier drinking once or twice per month. Prefers to continue working despite symptoms.

Examination:
- Vitals:
- Examination findings:

Impression:
- Acute gastroenteritis (likely infectious), with high stool frequency and risk of dehydration. Contact history noted (brother with similar illness).

Plan:
- Hydration: Encourage clear fluids; use oral rehydration solution (e.g., Dioralyte) over-the-counter.
- Diet: Start with clear fluids and soft diet (e.g., soup, mashed foods); advance as tolerated.
- Symptom relief: Paracetamol/acetaminophen as needed for fever/pain (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Lifestyle: Avoid alcohol during recovery.
- Follow-up/safety-net: If not improving within 48 hours, contact clinic for reassessment; if signs of dehydration progress, further investigations may be needed.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: No vitals or physical exam documented; no objective temperature; hydration status not objectively assessed; stool characteristics beyond “watery” not fully characterized; no recent travel/antibiotics/food exposure history documented; no guidance on work/sick note; medication dosing not documented; allergies confirmed but broader medication reconciliation limited.
- Internal conflicts: Doctor stated “feeling hoarse,” while patient reported feeling hot/feverish; no hoarseness otherwise discussed (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: Occasional audio/connection issues and interruptions; some unclear or incomplete statements.
